1. The animation shows the trade-off between paying extra on a mortgage and using that cash for something else. An illustrative homeowner, Tessa, holds a banknote beside her house. The mortgage rate, 7.40% a year before taxes, is set up as a "bar" that any other use of the money would have to clear. The rate is labeled as the Oct 8, 2026 survey rate.

2. The banknote starts beside Tessa and then moves up onto a horizontal bar. A scale appears next to the bar with "zero" at the bottom and "7.40%" at the top. The house and Tessa shift position on screen, and the label "interest no longer charged" appears under the bar. In the last frames a second, dashed-outline banknote appears labeled "any other use," and then "not tested."

3. Money put toward the mortgage saves the interest that would otherwise be charged, which is the same as earning 7.40% a year before taxes. An alternative use of the cash would have to beat that figure to come out ahead. The animation does not test whether any alternative does. The dashed, faded banknote and the "not tested" label say so directly.

4. A viewer would probably take away only a framing, not a firm instruction. Extra payments have a known return equal to the loan rate, and investing is an unknown that has to be compared against that return. The animation does not say to prepay or to invest. The screen text says "ILLUSTRATIVE" and "US only · history, not a forecast," which also warns against reading it as a prediction.

5. The framing is the animation's own: the "bar" label, "interest no longer charged," and "any other use / not tested" are all on screen. Any advice beyond that, such as "prepay if you're stretched," is my conclusion and does not come from the animation. Applying it to your $320,000 mortgage, a 15-year term and your tax situation would need your actual rate and numbers.
